# Abstract

This study examines the association between prenatal mental health screening and postpartum depressive symptoms using data from the Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System (PRAMS) Phase 8. The analysis focuses on self reported prenatal care experiences and postpartum mental health outcomes. Descriptive statistics and multivariable logistic regression were used to evaluate whether screening is associated with differences in reported depressive symptoms while adjusting for key covariates. Prenatal mental health screening was associated with lower odds of postpartum depressive symptoms, although the magnitude of the association was modest. Findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the observational and self reported nature of the data.

# Introduction

Postpartum depression is a significant public health concern that affects maternal well being, family functioning, and infant outcomes @bauman2020vitalsigns. Clinical guidelines increasingly recommend routine screening for depression and anxiety during pregnancy and the postpartum period @acog2023screening @uspstf2019perinatal.

Despite these recommendations, it remains unclear whether prenatal mental health screening is associated with postpartum depressive symptoms in real world population settings. Most existing evidence focuses on clinical or intervention based settings, with less emphasis on population based surveillance data.

Using PRAMS Phase 8 data, this study evaluates whether individuals who report being asked about depression or anxiety during prenatal care are less likely to report postpartum depressive symptoms.

## General Background Information

Prenatal and postpartum mental health conditions are increasingly recognized as critical components of maternal health. Poor maternal mental health has been associated with adverse outcomes for both mothers and infants, including reduced maternal functioning and challenges in early child development @acog2023screening. As a result, healthcare providers are encouraged to assess mental health concerns throughout pregnancy and after delivery.

Routine screening for depression during pregnancy may provide opportunities for earlier identification of individuals experiencing symptoms or those at elevated risk of developing postpartum depression. However, population level evidence examining how prenatal screening relates to postpartum depressive symptoms remains limited. Understanding this relationship may help inform both clinical practice and maternal health policy.

## Description of Data

The data for this study come from the Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System, or PRAMS, Phase 8, a population based surveillance system conducted by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in collaboration with state health departments @cdc_prams_phase8_codebook @cdc_prams_phase8_topics. PRAMS collects self reported survey data from individuals who recently had a live birth and links these responses to selected birth certificate variables.

PRAMS is designed to monitor maternal experiences and behaviors before, during, and shortly after pregnancy. The survey includes questions related to prenatal care, maternal health conditions, health behaviors, mental health, and postpartum experiences. These data allow researchers to examine population level patterns related to maternal and infant health.

PRAMS Phase 8 includes several hundred variables capturing maternal demographics, pre pregnancy health conditions, prenatal care experiences, health behaviors, insurance coverage, mental health indicators, and postpartum outcomes. The dataset contains a mix of categorical and numeric variables and reflects real world survey complexity, including skip patterns and missing data.

## Research Question

The primary research question for this study is:

Are individuals who report being asked about depression or anxiety during prenatal care less likely to report postpartum depressive symptoms?

# Methods

ChatGPT was used to assist with code troubleshooting and writing support. All code and analytical decisions were reviewed, revised as needed, and implemented by the author. The author takes full responsibility for the accuracy, interpretation, and reproducibility of the work presented here.

## Data Source

Data were obtained from PRAMS, a population based surveillance system conducted by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention in collaboration with state health departments. PRAMS collects self reported information on maternal experiences before, during, and shortly after pregnancy.

## Study Population

The full PRAMS analytic dataset included 237,392 respondents. After excluding observations with missing values for the primary exposure, outcome, and selected covariates used in the main model, the final analytic sample included 233,213 respondents.

## Measures

The primary exposure was self reported prenatal mental health screening, measured using a PRAMS survey item indicating whether a healthcare provider asked about depression or anxiety during prenatal care.

The primary outcome was postpartum depressive symptoms. PRAMS includes survey items assessing whether respondents experienced feelings consistent with depression or loss of interest following childbirth. These items have been used in previous research examining postpartum depressive symptoms using PRAMS data @bauman2020vitalsigns @farr2016provider.

Key covariates included prior depression during pregnancy and maternal education.

## Statistical Approach

Exploratory analyses included descriptive statistics, cross tabulations, and graphical comparisons of postpartum depressive symptoms by screening status. Multivariable logistic regression models were used to evaluate the association between prenatal mental health screening and postpartum depressive symptoms while adjusting for depression during pregnancy and maternal education.

# Results

Overall, 81.1% of respondents reported being screened for depression during prenatal care, and 14.2% reported postpartum depressive symptoms.

## Exploratory Analysis

We first examined the distribution of prenatal mental health screening and postpartum depressive symptoms in the analytic sample. Preliminary descriptive results suggested that postpartum depressive symptoms were slightly less common among respondents who reported receiving prenatal mental health screening.

```{r}
knitr::include_graphics("figures/screening_vs_postpartum_depression.png")
```

Figure 1 shows that individuals who reported receiving prenatal mental health screening had a slightly lower prevalence of postpartum depressive symptoms than those who were not screened.

```{r}
screening_summary <- read_csv("tables/screening_summary.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
knitr::kable(
  screening_summary,
  caption = "Table 2. Distribution of postpartum depressive symptoms by prenatal mental health screening"
)
```

Table 2 shows that among respondents who were not screened during prenatal care, 15.2% reported postpartum depressive symptoms. Among those who were screened, 13.9% reported postpartum depressive symptoms.

## Multivariable Analysis

```{r}
multi_clean <- tibble(
  Predictor = c(
    "Screened during prenatal care",
    "Depression during pregnancy",
    "High school graduate",
    "Some college",
    "College graduate",
    "More than college"
  ),
  `Odds ratio` = c(0.76, 3.38, 1.36, 1.29, 1.09, 0.69),
  `95% CI` = c(
    "(0.74, 0.78)",
    "(3.29, 3.47)",
    "(1.25, 1.48)",
    "(1.19, 1.40)",
    "(1.01, 1.18)",
    "(0.64, 0.75)"
  ),
  `P value` = c("<0.001", "<0.001", "<0.001", "<0.001", "0.034", "<0.001")
)

knitr::kable(
  multi_clean,
  caption = "Table 3. Adjusted odds ratios for postpartum depressive symptoms"
)
```

In adjusted analyses, prenatal mental health screening was associated with lower odds of postpartum depressive symptoms. Prior depression during pregnancy remained the strongest predictor of postpartum depressive symptoms.

## Model Validation

```{r}
model_tbl <- read_csv("tables/model_comparison.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
knitr::kable(
  model_tbl,
  caption = "Table 4. Cross validation model comparison"
)
```

Logistic regression and random forest models demonstrated similar predictive performance, suggesting that more complex machine learning approaches did not substantially improve performance relative to the simpler regression model.

# Discussion

This study evaluated the association between prenatal mental health screening and postpartum depressive symptoms using population based PRAMS data. Results suggest that individuals who reported receiving prenatal screening had slightly lower rates of postpartum depressive symptoms, even after adjustment for key covariates.

These findings are generally consistent with existing research showing that postpartum depressive symptoms remain a significant public health concern in the United States @bauman2020vitalsigns @farr2016provider. Clinical guidelines also recommend routine screening for depression during pregnancy and the postpartum period to support earlier identification and intervention @acog2023screening.

The exploratory results suggest that prenatal screening may be associated with differences in postpartum mental health outcomes at the population level. However, these results should be interpreted cautiously. Because the data are observational and based on self reported survey responses, the analyses cannot determine whether prenatal screening itself reduces postpartum depressive symptoms.

Prior depression during pregnancy emerged as one of the strongest predictors of postpartum depressive symptoms. This finding aligns with prior research showing that mental health history is an important risk factor for postpartum depression.

## Limitations

This study has several limitations. PRAMS data are self reported and may be subject to recall bias or reporting bias. The postpartum depressive symptom measure used in PRAMS is not a clinical diagnosis but rather a survey based indicator of depressive symptoms. In addition, the observational design limits causal interpretation. Unmeasured factors such as healthcare access, provider practices, or social support may influence both screening and postpartum mental health outcomes.

## Conclusion

This study demonstrates how large surveillance datasets such as PRAMS can be used to explore maternal mental health patterns and generate hypotheses for future research. Continued attention to perinatal mental health remains important for improving maternal and infant health outcomes.
